narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 55.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is slightly more than a coin-flip risk, not a certainty, but it was enough for the school to treat your application as too risky under its review process.

The strongest factor driving that prediction was your LSAT score. At 27, it is well below the average of about 37 among accepted students, and it pushed the estimate toward bar-exam failure more than any other information. The next most important factor was your undergraduate GPA. This worked in your favor: at 3.80, it is above the accepted-student average of 3.23, and it pushed the prediction toward passing. The third most influential factor was your third-year class-rank decile. At 4.00, compared with an average of 5.79 among accepted students, it suggested lower relative academic standing in that year and pushed the prediction back toward failure. In short, your strong GPA helped you, but it was outweighed by the LSAT score and third-year rank.

To improve your chances, focus first on retaking the LSAT after serious preparation and ask admissions whether an updated score would be considered. You should also provide context for your third-year rank, such as an upward trend or unusual circumstances, and consider reapplying after a stronger LSAT result or additional academic work that demonstrates readiness.
